records.title: The BspC surface adhesin and gastrointestinal fungal colonization enhance group B streptococcal neonatal infection.
records.abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonizes the gastrointestinal (GI) and female reproductive tracts of up to 30% of healthy adults, but during pregnancy can be transmitted to the newborn, causing neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. Neonatal GI colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the mechanisms governing GBS intestinal persistence and dissemination are still being elucidated. Given the predominance of hypervirulent sequence type 17 (ST-17) strains in neonatal invasive disease, we hypothesized that the ST-17-associated surface adhesin BspC contributes to gastrointestinal colonization and infection. Using a neonatal mouse model, we found that pups infected with wild-type GBS exhibited increased mortality and significantly higher bacterial burdens in the intestine, blood, spleen, and brain compared with pups infected with a ΔbspC mutant. We also observed that BspC promoted adherence to a 2D organoid model of the human infant colon and Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells through its variable domain. Building on previous findings that Candida albicans interacts with BspC, we found that C. albicans enhanced GBS intestinal epithelial adherence in a BspC-dependent manner, and coinfection increased intestinal GBS burden and brain dissemination in neonatal mice. Finally, analysis of published human neonatal fecal microbiome data sets revealed higher GBS abundance in infants colonized with C. albicans or other Candida species. Together, these findings identify BspC as a key mediator of GBS intestinal colonization and invasive disease and suggest that fungal colonization of the neonatal GI promotes GBS pathogenesis.IMPORTANCEGroup B Streptococcus (GBS) is a leading cause of neonatal infection, which can result in fatality or long-term neurological morbidity in survivors. Intestinal colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the factors that promote GBS persistence in the neonatal gastrointestinal tract remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the GBS surface adhesin BspC as a mediator of intestinal epithelial adherence, gastrointestinal colonization, and systemic dissemination. We further demonstrate that the common fungal pathobiont Candida albicans enhances GBS intestinal adherence and infection. Consistent with our experimental findings, analysis of human infant microbiome data sets revealed greater GBS abundance in infants colonized with Candida species. These findings identify BspC as a key mediator of this process and suggest that fungal colonization can enhance GBS disease.

records.title: In vitro efficacy of synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33 against poultry isolates with diverse antimicrobial resistance phenotypes.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an impactful One Health issue. One of its drivers is the extensive use of antibiotics in both human and animal production systems, and despite regulatory restrictions on antibiotic use in poultry farming, antimicrobial resistance remains a major challenge. Consequently, animals are at higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs, highlighting the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. Toward this end, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum activity and lower propensity to induce resistance. However, the effectiveness of AMPs against poultry pathogens, and in particular multidrug-resistant strains, is largely unclear. Here, we evaluated SET-M33, a synthetic tetrabranched AMP, against four species of clinically relevant pathogens in poultry, namely, Escherichia coli, Salmonella enterica, Enterococcus faecalis, and Enterococcus cecorum. Using a panel of 141 field isolates, we found that SET-M33 broadly inhibited bacterial growth at low micromolar concentrations (median minimum inhibitory concentrations of 2.5 and 5 μM for gram-negative and gram-positive strains, respectively), including in multidrug-resistant isolates. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on host cells, we established an in vitro co-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability. These findings demonstrate the potential of SET-M33 as a new antimicrobial agent against pathogens in poultry. Antimicrobial resistance is an important One Health issue that affects human and animal health. In particular, antimicrobial resistance remains a challenge in poultry farming, where animals are at a higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs. To solve this issue, we need alternative antimicrobial strategies, and antimicrobial peptides have emerged as particularly promising candidates. Here, we examined the efficacy of one such new antimicrobial, the synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33, against a large panel of poultry pathogen isolates. We found that SET-M33 was highly effective against the vast majority of isolates, including strains that are multidrug resistant or resistant to other antimicrobial peptides. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on the host, we established an in vitro co-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability.

records.title: [Research progress in the construction of prostate organoid model].
records.abstract: Prostate organoids are highly biomimetic in vitro models that serve as platforms for pathological simulation and therapeutic validation in precision medicine. The traditional three-dimensional (3D) culture system achieves organoid formation by taking advantage of the self-organizing characteristics of stem cells and relying on their autonomous assembly ability, with very little external regulatory input. However, this strategy has significant limitations in the construction of spatial heterogeneity and the simulation of dynamic microenvironments. The integration of bioengineering and stem cell technology has given rise to biomimetic strategies based on advanced technologies such as programmable biomaterials, organ-on-a-chip devices and bioprinting, which will enable spatiotemporal controllable physicochemical intervention. This review summarizes current construction frameworks, highlights the pivotal role of engineered strategies in enhancing physiological relevance, and discusses the transformative potential of artificial intelligence -driven models, aiming to advance the development of high-fidelity prostate organoids.

records.title: Residual disease as a therapy-remodeled ecosystem: spatial niches, tumor persistence, and relapse in solid tumors.
records.abstract: Residual disease comprises the malignant burden that remains after treatment, including low-volume lesions and clinically occult reservoirs. Surviving cells encounter a tissue environment altered by cell death, inflammation, repair, stromal activation, vascular injury, and metabolic stress. These changes can support spatially restricted persistence, but co-localization alone does not establish a protective niche. This narrative review links therapy-associated tissue remodeling to the location and state of residual cells and to the timing of potential relapse-directed intervention. We distinguish molecular residual disease, treatment-tolerant persister states, dormancy, and stable resistance, and separate selection of pre-existing populations from experimentally demonstrated state induction. Across chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, endocrine therapy, and immunotherapy, we distinguish human observational or trial evidence from mechanistic findings in mouse models, organoids, and cell culture. We organize niche evidence into spatial enrichment, association with a residual-cell state, selective perturbation, and an effect on reactivation or relapse. Examples illustrate dose-dependent radiation responses, multifactorial stromal protection, context-dependent immune surveillance, and collateral metabolic vulnerabilities. Longitudinal spatial profiling, lineage analysis, spatial pharmacology, and clinically informative circulating tumor DNA studies offer complementary information; molecular detection does not identify a particular tissue niche or directly demonstrate viable residual cells. Four therapeutic windows are proposed as research strategies rather than a validated clinical classification. Their utility depends on the interaction being required, the drug reaching the relevant region, and acceptable effects on normal repair and tumor-restraining functions. Limited paired human sampling and the compressed timescale of experimental models remain major constraints on translation.

records.title: [Research progress and clinical applications of thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy models].
records.abstract: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) is the most common orbital disease in adults, an organ-specific autoimmune disorder that severely impairs patients' visual function and quality of life. To investigate its pathogenesis and explore therapeutic strategies, various experimental models have been developed. This article systematically reviews the evolution of TAO models, ranging from early pituitary extract injection, cell-mediated immunization, and gene immunization models, to adenoviral immunization and novel three-dimensional (3D) organoid models. It summarizes research progress of these models in immune mechanisms and fibrosis regulation, and analyzes the challenges of current models, including insufficient phenotypic reproducibility, imperfect simulation of immune responses, and poor clinical relevance. Finally, it prospects the potential of combined application of multiple models, optimization of modeling techniques, and humanized development. Despite these challenges, TAO experimental models show great promise for elucidating disease mechanisms and developing personalized therapies.

records.title: Functional Construction Strategies and Multidimensional Applications of Kidney Organoids.
records.abstract: Kidney diseases represent a major global health burden, highlighting the need for advanced human-relevant models to investigate disease mechanisms and develop therapeutic strategies. Stem cell-derived kidney organoids have emerged as powerful human-relevant platforms that recapitulate key aspects of kidney development and enable the modeling of renal diseases. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in kidney organoid construction and characterization and highlights key bioengineering strategies for improving their structural and functional properties. These strategies include decellularized extracellular matrix scaffolds, 3D bioprinting, genetic engineering, vascularization, and organoid-on-a-chip technologies. Their broad biomedical applications in disease modeling, drug screening, toxicity assessment, and regenerative medicine are further discussed. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are addressed, with emphasis on improving reproducibility, maturation, and functional relevance to advance the translational potential of kidney organoids.

records.title: Virtual metrology for process perturbation prediction in lithographic alignment marks using a physics-guided directed attention network.
records.abstract: Process perturbations in lithographic alignment marks deform multilayer profiles, break mark symmetry, and introduce alignment position uncertainty. Although alignment position deviation (APD) and wafer quality (WQ) responses contain process-dependent information, retrieving the underlying perturbations remains challenging because the inverse relationship is nonlinear and strongly coupled. We formulate this task as alignment mark virtual metrology, in which process perturbation values are estimated from paired APD/WQ response matrices. To solve this inverse problem, we propose a physics-guided directed attention network (PG-DAN). PG-DAN uses diffraction limit masked attention (DLMA) to inject wavelength, diffraction order, propagation, locality, and identity priors into APD/WQ attention logits, enabling the model to use physically meaningful token relations rather than unconstrained data correlations. A directed decoder further follows multilayer coupling during prediction. Evaluated on a rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) dataset, PG-DAN achieves a mean R2 of 0.999875, a mean range-normalized RMSE of 0.34%, and a mean range-normalized MAE of 0.23%, with lower estimation errors than conventional neural inverse models. These results support physics-guided inverse modeling for alignment mark process perturbation estimation.

records.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

records.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
records.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.

records.title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models.
records.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model's assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.

records.title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
records.abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

records.title: The Tenocyte from Atom to Cell: A Critical Multiscale Synthesis Linking Collagen Chemistry, Tissue Mechanics, Cell Mechanobiology and Mathematical Modelling.
records.abstract: The tenocyte builds, maintains, senses and degrades one of the most mechanically demanding extracellular matrices in vertebrates, yet the chemical, physical, biological and mathematical descriptions of this system have developed in largely separate literatures. This review examines the tenocyte-matrix unit as a single causal system spanning eight orders of magnitude in length, organised around five transitions: from collagen chemistry to molecular mechanics; from molecule to fibril and fascicle; from tissue loading to the cellular mechanical stimulus; from stimulus to transcription; and from cellular output back to matrix composition. At each transition, we weigh competing hypotheses, identify where evidence is decisive and where it remains correlative, and state the governing equations. We integrate advances from 2021-2026, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of human tendons, the establishment of PIEZO1 as a causal regulator of tendon stiffness, and microstructurally derived constitutive models. We argue that tendon homeostasis is a closed-loop control problem, formalised as a mechanostat with an inverted-U dose-response, and that the recurrent pathologies of tendon-tendinopathy, ageing, diabetic stiffening and fibrotic healing are failures of this loop rather than of any single component. An open-source computational companion (tenocyte-virtual-cell) is introduced, and a prioritised research agenda closes the review.

records.title: PFM: perturbed flow matching for structure-based drug design.
records.abstract: Target-specific 3D molecular generation is a promising approach for structure-based drug design. However, existing diffusion-based methods are generally restricted to marginal distributions with closed-form solutions, limiting the flexibility of generative process design, especially for the forward noising process. As a result, these methods may be less effective in modeling the complex distributions underlying pocket-conditioned molecular generation. We develop Perturbed Flow Matching (PFM), a flow-matching-based framework for protein pocket-conditioned 3D molecular generation. PFM employs a perturbed conditional probability path that incorporates both pocket binding-site information and coupled atom type-coordinate information, enabling more effective generation of molecules in protein binding environments. On CrossDocked2020, PFM achieves competitive structural quality and the best average Vina score among the evaluated unguided methods (-7.12); PFM-G further improves the score to -8.70 with tailored classifier-free guidance. Experiments on additional molecular datasets further confirm the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed framework. https://github.com/kurisu92725/PFM.

records.title: De novo design of miniprotein inhibitors of bacterial adhesins.
records.abstract: The rise of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections necessitates the discovery of novel antimicrobial strategies. Here, we show that protein design provides a generalizable means of generating new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins, which are virulence factors critical in host-pathogen interactions. We de novo designed high-affinity miniprotein binders to FimH and Abp chaperone usher pili adhesins from uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii, respectively, which are implicated in mediating both uncomplicated and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI) responsible for significant morbidity worldwide. The designed antagonists have high specificity and stability, disrupt bacterial recognition of host receptors, block biofilm formation, and are effective in treating and preventing murine models of uncomplicated and catheter-associated UTIs in vivo.

records.title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design.
records.abstract: Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

records.title: Programming Targeted Immune Cell Migration Using Orthogonal Chemokine-Receptor Pairs.
records.abstract: Chemokines orchestrate the migration of immune cells throughout the body, but harnessing chemokine signaling to engineer targeted cell trafficking is challenging because of their overlapping interactions and broad expression patterns. Here we used structure-guided protein design to engineer orthogonal chemokine-receptor pairs with minimal crosstalk to native systems. T cells engineered with an ortho-receptor selectively infiltrated tissues producing the ortho-chemokine, in vitro and in vivo. By engineering T cells that both sense and secrete the ortho-chemokine, we generated collective swarming behavior in which pioneer cells attract follower cells via an ortho-chemokine gradient self-organized by positive feedback. By providing orthogonal genetic control over both the generation and sensing of chemokine gradients, this system enables the construction of autonomous spatial targeting programs in engineered cells.

records.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing.
records.abstract: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) [1] with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN [2], AlphaFold3 (AF3) [3], and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperone's utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone .

records.title: MYC targeted de novo binders impair tumor growth.
records.abstract: MYC is one of the most frequently dysregulated oncogenic drivers across many cancers, yet direct therapeutic targeting has remained difficult because its function is mediated by disordered regions and transient protein-protein interactions. Here we design proteins that bind epitopes within regions of MYC whose sequence is conserved between human and mouse, including intrinsically disordered motifs required for oncogenic activity. In vitro, the designs bind MYC with nanomolar affinity and in cells they engage MYC, disrupt interactions with MAX, and remodel MYC-associated protein complexes. Expression of the binders decreases cell proliferation across diverse MYC-dependent hematopoietic, liver, pancreatic, and patient-derived tumor models, and in an orthotopic pancreatic cancer model, binder-expressing tumor cells were selectively depleted. This work establishes de novo protein design as a generalizable strategy to therapeutically target intrinsically disordered transcription factors. We developed a panel of de novo designed intracellular protein binders that target conserved functional regions of MYC with nanomolar affinity, remodel MYC complexes and interaction networks in cells, suppress proliferation across MYC-dependent cancer models, and are depleted from orthotopic pancreatic tumors in vivo.

records.title: Long-term economic benefits of early cancer detection through enhanced multimodal screening: a modeling study of whole-body MRI and liquid biopsy.
records.abstract: Aim: Cancer poses a substantial health and economic burden in the US Although early detection is associated with improved outcomes and lower treatment costs, many cancers are still diagnosed at advanced stages. Enhanced multimodal screening combining whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB MRI) and blood-based multicancer early detection (MCED) may shift diagnoses earlier, but its long-term economic impact remains uncertain. Materials & methods: We developed an economic model to estimate expected cancer-related costs under two scenarios: status quo with conventional screening and enhanced multimodal screening incorporating WB MRI and MCED. The analysis included common cancers with an annual incidence of ≥10,000 new cases in the US in 2025. Expected cancer management costs were estimated using incidence-based 5-year stage-specific medical costs. Productivity losses were estimated using a simplified human capital approach, applying published stage-specific work-loss durations to sex-specific annual earnings. Under the intervention arm, conservative, moderate and maximum cancer stage-shift assumptions were evaluated. These scenarios reflected increasing degrees of earlier cancer detection, with a greater proportion of cancers assumed to be diagnosed at earlier stages rather than at advanced stages. Total expected cancer-related costs per person were derived by combining direct medical costs and productivity losses, weighted by cancer risk and stage distribution. Results: Under the status quo, expected cancer-related costs were estimated at $74,431 for men and $78,818 for women. With enhanced multimodal screening under the moderate stage-shift assumption, costs, including screening and false positive workup, declined to about $66,000 and $69,500, respectively, representing approximately 12% reduction. Under the conservative stage-shift assumption, total costs were similar to those under the status quo, whereas under the maximum stage-shift assumption, cost reductions ranged from 24.0% to 24.3% for men and from 24.7% to 25.0% for women. Conclusion: Enhanced multimodal screening may reduce the economic burden of cancer by shifting diagnosis toward earlier stages, although the magnitude of benefit depends substantially on the extent to which cancers are detected at earlier stages in practice. These findings highlight the potential long-term economic value of earlier cancer detection while underscoring the need for prospective evidence on the real-world performance of WB-MRI and MCED screening strategies. Because long-term real-world data for population-level WB-MRI and MCED screening remain limited, these findings should be interpreted as estimates of potential economic impact rather than projections of a specific screening program.

records.title: From histopathology to molecular taxonomy: predicting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors invasiveness.
records.abstract: Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs) are among the most prevalent intracranial tumors in adults. Although most follow an indolent clinical course, a substantial subset exhibits local invasion, which can limit gross total resection and increase the risk of residual disease and recurrence. Importantly, anatomical invasiveness should not be equated with clinical aggressiveness. Aggressive PitNETs may also exhibit a longitudinal pattern of repeated or multiple local recurrences and frequently require multiple therapeutic interventions. The 2022 Fifth Edition of the WHO Classification formally renamed pituitary adenomas to PitNETs and established a lineage classification framework centered on core transcription factors, including PIT1, TPIT, and SF1, thereby driving the transition from traditional pathological diagnosis to molecular subtyping. Driven by recent advances in high-throughput sequencing, liquid biopsy, and single-cell omics, numerous novel molecular biomarkers have emerged, enabling the early pre- and postoperative identification of invasive subpopulations. This review systematically outlines recent progress in multidimensional biomarkers-including DNA methylation, protein markers, non-coding RNAs, liquid biopsy indicators, and tumor microenvironmental features-to provide an updated synthesis of candidate biomarkers that may support future risk stratification and individualized management of invasive PitNETs.

records.title: From discordance to clinical decision support: integrating longitudinal imaging and ctDNA through multimodal artificial intelligence in precision oncology.
records.abstract: Accurate treatment-response assessment increasingly requires information that is spatial, molecular, and longitudinal. Imaging depicts lesion burden, anatomical distribution, and morphological evolution, whereas circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) provides a systemic molecular signal shaped by tumor shedding, clonal composition, assay characteristics, and treatment pressure. Because these modalities measure non-identical dimensions, disagreement between them is clinically plausible and can reflect lead-lag kinetics, site-specific progression, clonal evolution, or technical uncertainty. In this focused narrative review, we synthesize evidence for imaging-ctDNA integration and propose a multidimensional, multilabel taxonomy of discordance spanning directional, temporal, spatial, molecular, and technical dimensions. We distinguish isolated from persistent discordance and emphasize exact temporal alignment, analytical confidence, and orthogonal confirmation. Current evidence supports prognostic complementarity and demonstrates measurable discordance across tumor types, but clinical actionability is context dependent. Randomized studies such as PADA-1 show that molecular-first treatment adaptation can be beneficial when a defined biomarker is linked to a validated intervention, whereas other trials illustrate that molecular detectability alone does not guarantee benefit from early treatment. We therefore frame multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) as an uncertainty-aware decision-support approach rather than an automated treatment selector. Future systems should preserve modality-specific information, handle irregular longitudinal sampling, quantify uncertainty, identify information gaps, and recommend evidence-matched reassessment. Prospective validation should prioritize clinical utility, harms, transportability, governance, and net benefit rather than discrimination alone.

records.title: CRISPR-enabled biosensing of cancer-associated DNA methylation in cell-free DNA: molecular architectures, molecular sampling constraints, and translational biosensor engineering.
records.abstract: DNA methylation in circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) provides cancer-associated and tissue-of-origin information complementary to mutation-based liquid biopsy. Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based sensing is challenging because 5-methylcytosine (5 mC) generally preserves Watson-Crick base pairing and is not inherently resolved by sequence-programmed CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins. This targeted narrative review examines how methylated and unmethylated molecules are distinguished and converted into Cas-readable outputs under fragmented, low-input cfDNA conditions. We organize the literature into four discrimination routes comprising sequence conversion, enzymatic gating, affinity-assisted recognition, and native-state Cas modulation. Engineered molecular transduction is considered separately as a downstream enabling layer. We compare readouts in terms of quantitative fidelity and integration requirements. Sequence-conversion and enzymatic-gating systems have the broadest analytical evidence among the identified studies, largely from in vitro experiments. Direct affinity-assisted 5 mC-to-Cas sensing remains sparsely studied, and evidence for native-state sensing in patient-derived cfDNA is limited to exploratory observational comparisons. No native-state Cas methylation assay identified in this review has established clinically usable diagnostic performance. Reported analytical limits of detection and methylation-fraction discrimination cannot be extrapolated to clinical sensitivity without accounting for input, recovery, fragmentation, background, and decision thresholds. Translation requires validated biomarkers, fragment-matched calibration, orthogonal reference testing, reproducible device integration, and independent evaluation of locked assays in intended-use populations.

records.title: Copper-Peptide Assemblies with Self-Driven Signal Release for Electrochemical Analysis of Exosomes.
records.abstract: Multifunctional peptides have garnered considerable attention owing to their excellent biocompatibility and unique physicochemical properties. Herein, we report an electrochemical method for the sensitive detection of exosomes based on copper-peptide assemblies with a self-driven signal release approach. In the design, an engineered histidine-rich peptide coordinates with Cu2+ to self-assemble into pH-responsive nanoparticles (Cu-Pep). Upon target exosome recognition, an aptamer-triggered terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated polymerization cascade is initiated. The protons generated during this process then lower the local pH, which in turn drives the autonomous disassembly of Cu-Pep and releases abundant Cu2+, producing a greatly amplified electrochemical signal readout. Benefiting from this ingenious self-driven cascade amplification, the method achieves an impressive limit of detection of 41 particles/μL, alongside outstanding selectivity and reproducibility. Furthermore, it can successfully differentiate exosomes among breast cancer patients, healthy controls, and post-treatment individuals in clinical serum samples, offering a powerful, non-invasive liquid biopsy strategy for diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of the cancer.

records.title: Exploiting Asymmetric Mismatch Sensitivity of Cas13a for Interference-Tolerant Single-CpG Methylation Analysis.
records.abstract: Accurate single-CpG methylation analysis in dense regions is critical for cancer diagnostics but challenged by adjacent CpG interference. Here, we developed EPICATCH, an interference-tolerant ratiometric Cas13a biosensor to overcome this limitation. Exploiting LbuCas13a's asymmetric mismatch sensitivity, we established a dual-zone recognition framework. Positioning the target CpG in the strictly sensitive 5'-zone guarantees single-base resolution, while placing adjacent CpGs in the tolerant 3'-zone masks epigenetic noise, achieving a 7-bp spatial resolution for the tested MYO1G construct. Integrated with recombinase polymerase amplification, ssDNA generation, and a dual-channel ratiometric readout, EPICATCH eliminates sample concentration biases, achieving a 100 aM limit of detection. Applying EPICATCH to quantify MYO1G methylation in clinical plasma cfDNA from colorectal cancer patients yielded a clinical sensitivity of 80.0% and specificity of 84.6%. This dual-zone recognition system provides a robust strategy for precise single-CpG analysis and cancer screening.
